doc.title: Art Farmer — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: George Russell as a person and the Lydian concept
summary: His patience in the studio, difficult meters, and Farmer's studies with him.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: What was it like working with George? What was he like as a person?

George was great. George is a great musician, but the thing that really impressed me about him was that he was very patient, and he never got excited and said, “Damn, you guys are awful. You’re messing up the music. Why does it take so long?” He never said nothing like that. It was always positive. He said, “Okay, let’s take it again” [laughs]. I don’t know how many times we would take it. Looking back, it seems ironic after spending weeks practicing alone, then you get into the recording studio and you still are not quite up to it. Then, you have to take one, take two, take three, take four. Finally, it’s all over, and I can listen to it now, and it sounds perfect. It sounds perfect. There’s no indication how difficult it was because this music was very hard. Later on, George got to the point where he got under the influence of Ornette Coleman where George would write a theme and then after theme, he would just let the soloists go free, but it wasn’t like that then. Whatever the form of the piece was, that’s what you had to base your solo on. Like if you wrote a piece that was nine bars of four-four and then three bars of five- four, that’s what you have to improvise on, and it wasn’t easy.
And at this time, he was developing his Lydian Chromatic Concepts.

He had developed that, and I wound up studying from him, which was very beneficial to me, but that was just from the harmony. Dealing with these various meters and improvising on them, that certainly wasn’t easy, I tell you. I don’t care what anybody says, it’s not easy.
